      "text": "## Verified findings\n\n- Attribute::TARGET_CLASS is the class-like target. PHP permits attributes on classes, interfaces, traits, and enums under this target; the manual groups these declarations as attribute targets. There is a version nuance: as of PHP 8.5, applying #[Attribute] itself to an abstract class, enum, interface, or trait is a compile-time error—this concerns declaring an attribute class, not using a TARGET_CLASS attribute on those declarations.\n- Reflection does not make attributes inherited automatically. ReflectionClass::getAttributes() returns attributes declared on the reflected class. To inspect a parent class’s declarations, walk the parent chain yourself. The ReflectionAttribute::IS_INSTANCEOF flag is for filtering attribute types by inheritance/implementation; it does not make the target class inherit a parent’s attributes.\n- Named constructor argument names are compatibility-sensitive. PHP stores named attribute arguments by name in reflection and passes them to the attribute constructor. Renaming a constructor parameter can therefore break consumers using that name in an attribute invocation, even if positional calls still work.\n\n## Roave BC-check scope\n\nThe primary Roave repository describes the tool as comparing two revisions of a PHP library’s class API to detect BC breaks; it does not, in the README material retrieved, substantiate the more specific claim about exclusions for @internal or namespaces named Internal.\nSo I cannot verify from the retrieved primary Roave source exactly how either exclusion works. The search surfaced secondary summaries and an issue, but those do not meet the primary-source-only constraint. Treat any blanket statement that Roave automatically excludes all @internal symbols or every Internal namespace as unverified until checked against the relevant implementation/version or its tests.\n\n## RFC 9457 implications\n\nRFC 9457 identifies a problem type by its type URI, which consumers must use as the primary identifier. It permits problem-specific extension members, and clients must ignore extensions they do not recognize. This makes an application-specific error code suitable as an extension member; the RFC does not prescribe that field or define its stability policy, so its meaning and compatibility guarantees belong to the API’s own contract.\nThe status body member is advisory and reports the status generated for that occurrence. If included, the generator must use the same status in the actual HTTP response; generic HTTP software follows the response status. New problem-type definitions must document the type URI, title, and associated HTTP status code.\nDesign classification: treat attribute constructor parameter names and documented error-code values as public contract when consumers are expected to use them. For HTTP errors, use the RFC problem type as the problem-kind identifier, keep the response status authoritative, and define any stable application error-code extension explicitly in the application’s own contract.\n\nSources:\n1. [github](https://github.com/Roave/BackwardCompatibilityCheck)\n2. [rfc-editor](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457)"
